text.p: Viacom Inc., one of the world's biggest entertainment and publishing companies, Wednesday posted a net loss of $19 million for the first quarter despite higher revenues.
The company, which owns Blockbuster video, Paramount studios, the MTV network and radio and television stations, posted a net loss of $18.7 million, or 10 cents a share, on revenues of $2.9 billion.
A year ago Viacom recorded a net profit of $27.8 million, or 3 cents a share, on revenues of $2.6 billion.

The loss, however, was smaller than Wall Street expected and Viacom stock gained on the American Stock Exchange. Its Class A common shares rose 69 cents to $28.94 while its Class B shares added 44 cents to $28.94 in active trading.
While revenues rose 11 percent, its cash flow -- earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization -- fell 13 percent to $392 million from $448 million.
Total operating income plunged 32 percent to $174 million from $256 million.

Viacom said its cash flow fell at three of its four main business segments, with only its Networks and Broadcasting unit, which includes the MTV, Nickelodeon and Showtime cable networks, posting an increase.

Viacom posted lower results its Video and Theme Parks unit mainly due to a weak performance by Blockbuster, which increased overall revenues through new store openings, although sales declined at stores opened for at least a year.

The video rental unit was hurt by what Viacom called "weaker video product" and increased rental tape expenses, as well as costs related to the relocation of Blockbuster's distribution centre and headquarters to Dallas.
But after straying from its core business at Blockbuster, Viacom is looking to get back to basics, officials said.

Rather than reshaping Blockbuster into a retail mecca stocked with popcorn and movie-character toys as well as videotapes, Viacom executives told financial analysts it was time to get back to the basic: video rentals.

In an hourlong conference call, Viacom offered little insight beyond that as to their strategy for the unit, analysts who took part said. It was their first call with the Wall Street community since Bill Fields, the former chairman and chief executive of Blockbuster, resigned last month.
"It is very clear they have yet to develop a strategy," Paine Webber analyst Christopher Dixon said.
Under Fields, a longtime retailing executive, Blockbuster was looking to become a convenience-style chain that offered an array of entertainment-related products.
The company has three market studies under way to try to come up with the right mix, analysts said Viacom Chief Executive Sumner Redstone Redstone told them.

The company is looking to cut costs by eliminating the middle man and self-distributing videos. In addition, it plans to buy fewer copies of videos it puts on its shelves, a purchase that can eat into revenues, analysts said.

But Viacom executives offered no further insight into how that strategy will evolve in a video-rental market that has softened as it competes against satellite TV, PCs and other at-home entertainment for consumers' time, analysts said.
"It's clearly not a Band-Aid situation," NatWest Securities analyst Gary Farber said. "The market that is there today is changing."
Viacom executives also did not say when they expected to name a successor to Fields.

The company said its earnings excluded contributions from Viacom Radio, which it is selling to Evergreen Corp. for $1.1 billion, interactive game operations, which it plans to dispose of by the end of 1997, and cable, split off last July.
